claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element automotive alloy containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios.
Co-doping the starting catalyst with Mo and Au can overcome activity loss.
Co-doping the starting catalyst with Mo and Au can improve catalyst durability.
The Mo/Au intervention maintains low platinum-group-metal consumption.
The intervention yields PtNiMoAu nanowires as the relevant structural mediator.
Mo suppresses the outward diffusion of Ni atoms in PtNi-based nanowires.
Au stabilizes the surface Pt overlayer in PtNi-based nanowires.
The Mo/Au-doped catalyst will outperform the untreated starting catalyst in activity.
The Mo/Au-doped catalyst will outperform the untreated starting catalyst in durability.
The improvements will persist during transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation.
The improvements will persist during exposure to H2O and NO.
The intervention mitigates degradation associated with thermal aging or increasing vehicle mileage.
The exact interaction between Mo and Au dopants in the PtNi catalyst is not fully understood.

A significant decrease in mass activity or electrochemically active surface area after 20,000 room-temperature acidic-electrolyte ADT cycles would decisively falsify the automotive-exhaust hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism is stated categorically as distinct Mo and Au functions, while the uncertainty field says their exact interaction is not fully understood; the hypothesis does not distinguish established individual effects from the uncertain combined interaction.

The claimed boundary is transient, low-temperature automotive exhaust with H2O, NO, thermal aging, and mileage effects, whereas the proposed decisive test is an oxygen-reduction ADT in room-temperature 0.1 M HClO4. Failure or success in that electrochemical environment is not decisive for the stated exhaust boundary.
